issues.legal_issue: A pending suit is not a proceeding with respect to property or a right transferred by a partition order merely because the dispute concerns property in the successor province or its taxing power.
material_facts: The suit sought to prevent an agricultural income-tax assessment concerning an estate situated in the territory that became the successor province.
The successor province's power to impose the tax arose from sovereign authority and the continuation of existing law, rather than from a transfer under the Rights, Property and Liabilities Order.
issues.conclusion: The suit was not with respect to property or a right transferred by the Rights, Property and Liabilities Order, so Article 12(2) did not apply on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Article 12(2) of the Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947 applies where the province succeeds, under that Order, to property, rights, or liabilities that are the subject of the proceedings. The estate's location in the successor province did not make the suit one with respect to transferred property; the taxing power passed as an incident of sovereignty under section 18(3) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, not by a transfer under the Order. The Court referred to Midnapore Zemindary Co. Ltd. v. Province of Bengal for the binding effect of the transition Orders.

predicates.pending_suit_about_taxing_action: A suit concerning a proposed taxing action was pending when the political transition occurred.
predicates.dispute_concerns_property_in_successor_t: The proposed tax concerned property situated in territory that became part of the successor province.
predicates.taxing_power_arose_from_sovereignty: The successor province's authority to impose the tax arose from sovereign power rather than a transfer of rights under the partition arrangements.

issues.definition: When a pending tax suit concerns property in a successor province but the taxing power arose from sovereignty rather than a transferred right, the property-or-rights basis for applying the substitution rule does not apply.

issues.legal_issue: A province's alleged liability to be restrained from completing an assessment commenced through an allegedly unauthorized notice can constitute liability in respect of an actionable wrong for purposes of allocating liabilities between successor provinces.
material_facts: An officer issued a notice requiring a return of agricultural income, commencing an assessment against a ruler who alleged that the taxing law was invalid as applied to him.
The suit was filed before any assessment had been made and sought declarations and an injunction to prevent the assessment from proceeding.

The alleged cause of action arose in the territory that became the successor province; the Court stated that if the cause of action did not arise wholly there, the successor province would still share liability jointly with the other province.
issues.conclusion: On the pleaded allegations, the former province was liable to be restrained from completing an allegedly illegal assessment, and that liability passed to the successor province under Article 10(2); if the cause of action did not arise wholly in the successor province, the liability was joint with the other province.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9(1)(b) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 empowered the Governor-General to allocate powers, rights, property, duties, and liabilities, and the Indian Independence (Rights, Property and Liabilities) Order, 1947 was to be construed broadly enough to avoid gaps in that allocation. Under Article 10(2)(a), a liability in respect of an actionable wrong passed to the province in whose territory the cause of action arose wholly; under Article 10(2)(c), other such liabilities were joint. A liability to be restrained by injunction from completing an allegedly illegal act already commenced can qualify, even though it is not limited to damages for a completed tort. The Court distinguished Raleigh Investment Co. Ltd. v. Governor-General in Council, where the suit in substance sought repayment and modification of an assessment already made.

rule.if: pending_suit_for_prospective_assessment_injunction and notice_commenced_assessment_process and plaintiff_alleged_assessment_was_unauthorized and (cause_arose_wholly_in_successor_territory or cause_spanned_territories)

predicates.pending_suit_for_prospective_assessment_: A suit was pending that sought to prevent a proposed assessment from proceeding.
predicates.notice_commenced_assessment_process: A tax official had issued a notice that began the assessment process.
predicates.plaintiff_alleged_assessment_was_unautho: The plaintiff alleged that the assessment was illegal or unauthorized as applied to the plaintiff.
predicates.cause_arose_wholly_in_successor_territor: The cause of action arose entirely in territory assigned to the successor province.
predicates.cause_spanned_territories: The cause of action did not arise entirely within the successor province's territory.

issues.definition: When a pending suit seeks to stop an assessment begun by notice on the ground that it is unauthorized, the successor province assumes the related liability alone if the cause arose wholly in its territory and jointly if the cause spanned territories.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory bar on suits to set aside or modify completed assessments does not bar a suit filed before assessment seeking prospective relief against an allegedly unauthorized assessment.
material_facts: The suit was instituted before any assessment had been made.
The relief sought included declarations about the validity of the taxing law and notice, and an injunction restraining the defendants from taking steps to assess the plaintiff.
issues.conclusion: Section 65 of the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1944 did not bar the suit because it was not a suit to set aside or modify an assessment already made.
issues.legal_principle: Section 65 of the Bengal Agricultural Income-tax Act, 1944 barred suits to set aside or modify an assessment made under the Act. The Court distinguished Raleigh Investment Co. Ltd. v. Governor-General in Council, where the claim in substance sought repayment of tax already assessed and paid; here, no assessment existed when the suit was filed, and the suit challenged the initiation of the assessment process and sought prospective relief.

predicates.civil_suit_challenges_proposed_assessmen: A civil suit challenges a proposed tax assessment.
predicates.no_assessment_existed_when_suit_was_file: No assessment had been made when the plaintiff filed the suit.
predicates.relief_seeks_to_prevent_assessment: The requested relief seeks to prevent the assessment process from proceeding rather than to set aside or modify a completed assessment.

issues.definition: A suit filed before an assessment exists is not barred when it challenges the proposed assessment and seeks to prevent it from proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A court where a proceeding was pending before partition retains jurisdiction to continue it against a successor province that assumes the former province's liability.
material_facts: The suit was pending in a civil court before partition and had originally been brought against the former province.
The successor province was substituted as defendant after the former province ceased to exist.
The successor province assumed the former province's liability in respect of the alleged actionable wrong.
issues.conclusion: The successor province was deemed substituted as a party, and the pending suit could continue in the court where it was pending.
issues.legal_principle: Article 4 of the Indian Independence (Legal Proceedings) Order, 1947 continued pending proceedings in the court where they were pending, with that court retaining its jurisdiction and powers. Read with Article 12(2) of the Rights, Property and Liabilities Order, the court could proceed against a province that succeeded to the relevant liability under Article 10(2). The transition Orders were made under section 9 of the Indian Independence Act, 1947; the Court referred to Midnapore Zemindary Co. Ltd. v. Province of Bengal concerning their binding effect.

predicates.civil_suit_pending_before_partition: A civil suit was pending in a court before a political partition took effect.
predicates.in_original_court: The suit remained pending in the court where it had been brought or transferred before the partition took effect.
predicates.successor_province_assumes_liability: A successor province assumed the former province's liability relating to the pending suit.

issues.definition: When a civil suit remains pending in its original court and the successor province assumes the relevant liability, that court may continue the suit against the successor.
